acne.overview: Acne is a common skin condition where hair follicles become clogged with oil and dead skin cells, leading to whiteheads, blackheads, pimples or deeper cysts. Possible triggers include hormones, certain skin products, stress and some medicines.
symptoms: Painful lumps under the skin in severe cases
precautions: Wash gently twice daily with a mild cleanser
Keep hair and phone screens clean
acne.when_to_see_doctor: See a dermatologist if acne is painful, leaves scars, or does not improve after a few weeks of over-the-counter care.

medicines.name: Benzoyl peroxide 2.5–5% gel
medicines.usage_note: Often used once daily on affected areas; may cause dryness at first.
medicines.caution: Can bleach fabrics; avoid eyes and lips.

medicines.name: Adapalene 0.1% gel (topical retinoid)
medicines.caution: Not recommended in pregnancy; increases sun sensitivity.

medicines.name: Clindamycin 1% gel (topical antibiotic)
medicines.usage_note: Generally combined with benzoyl peroxide to reduce resistance.
medicines.caution: Use only when clinically indicated and under professional guidance.

eczema.overview: Eczema is a long-term condition that makes skin dry, itchy and inflamed. It often comes in flares and can be triggered by soaps, weather changes, allergens or stress.
precautions: Use fragrance-free soaps and lukewarm water
eczema.when_to_see_doctor: See a doctor if itching disturbs sleep, the skin looks infected (yellow crusts, pus) or flares are frequent.

medicines.name: Emollient / fragrance-free moisturiser
medicines.usage_note: Applied generously and often, especially after bathing.
medicines.caution: Choose products without fragrance or dyes.

medicines.name: Hydrocortisone 1% cream (mild steroid)
medicines.caution: Avoid long-term use on face or thin skin without advice.

medicines.name: Cetirizine (oral antihistamine)
medicines.usage_note: May help with itch-related sleep disturbance.
medicines.caution: Can cause drowsiness; check dosing for children.

psoriasis.overview: Psoriasis is an immune-related condition that speeds up skin cell turnover, causing thick, scaly plaques, often on elbows, knees, scalp and lower back.
symptoms: Raised, thickened patches with silvery scales
precautions: Avoid skin injury and harsh scrubbing
Get modest sun exposure as advised by a doctor
psoriasis.when_to_see_doctor: See a dermatologist for diagnosis and long-term management, or if joints become painful or swollen.

medicines.name: Coal tar or salicylic acid preparations
medicines.caution: May irritate; tar can stain.

medicines.name: Topical corticosteroids (e.g. betamethasone)
medicines.usage_note: Used for plaques in short courses.
medicines.caution: Potency must match the body area; avoid prolonged use.

medicines.name: Calcipotriol (vitamin D analogue)
medicines.caution: Avoid face and skin folds unless advised.

rosacea.overview: Rosacea is a chronic condition causing facial redness, visible blood vessels and sometimes acne-like bumps, usually on the cheeks, nose and forehead.
precautions: Avoid triggers such as spicy food, alcohol and heat
Use gentle skincare without alcohol or menthol
rosacea.when_to_see_doctor: See a dermatologist if redness is persistent, eyes are irritated, or the nose thickens.

medicines.name: Metronidazole 0.75% gel
medicines.caution: Results usually take several weeks.

medicines.name: Azelaic acid 15–20%
medicines.caution: May sting initially.

medicines.name: Broad-spectrum sunscreen SPF 30+
medicines.caution: Prefer mineral (zinc/titanium) formulas for sensitive skin.

melasma.overview: Melasma causes brown or grey-brown patches, mainly on the face. It is linked to sun exposure, hormones (pregnancy, contraceptives) and genetics.
symptoms: Symmetrical brown patches on cheeks, forehead or upper lip
precautions: Avoid harsh bleaching creams of unknown content
Discuss hormonal medicines with a doctor
melasma.when_to_see_doctor: See a dermatologist to confirm the diagnosis and before using lightening agents.

medicines.name: Broad-spectrum tinted sunscreen SPF 50
medicines.usage_note: Cornerstone of treatment; reapply every 2–3 hours outdoors.
medicines.caution: Iron-oxide tinted formulas block visible light too.

medicines.name: Azelaic acid 20%
medicines.caution: May cause mild irritation.

medicines.name: Hydroquinone 2–4%
medicines.caution: Avoid unsupervised or long-term use; risk of ochronosis.

tinea.overview: Tinea (ringworm) is a fungal infection causing ring-shaped, itchy, scaly patches. It is common in hot, humid climates and spreads through contact and shared items.
symptoms: Ring-shaped red patch with clearer centre
Patches in groin, feet or body folds
precautions: Do not share towels or clothes
tinea.when_to_see_doctor: See a doctor if it spreads widely, affects scalp or nails, or does not improve after 2 weeks.

medicines.name: Clotrimazole 1% cream
medicines.usage_note: Usually applied twice daily and continued 1–2 weeks after clearing.
medicines.caution: Stopping early can cause recurrence.

medicines.name: Terbinafine 1% cream
medicines.caution: Avoid combination steroid-antifungal creams without advice.

medicines.name: Oral antifungals (e.g. terbinafine, itraconazole)
medicines.caution: Need medical assessment; may affect liver.

vitiligo.overview: Vitiligo is a condition in which pigment-producing cells are lost, leaving smooth white patches. It is not contagious and its course varies between people.
symptoms: Premature whitening of hair in affected areas
precautions: Avoid skin injury which can trigger new patches
vitiligo.when_to_see_doctor: See a dermatologist for confirmation and to discuss treatment options early.

medicines.name: Broad-spectrum sunscreen SPF 50
medicines.caution: Reapply regularly.

medicines.name: Topical corticosteroids
medicines.usage_note: May help repigmentation in limited patches.
medicines.caution: Requires supervision to avoid thinning.

medicines.name: Tacrolimus 0.1% ointment
medicines.usage_note: Often used for face and neck.
medicines.caution: May cause burning sensation initially.

warts.overview: Warts are small, rough growths caused by human papillomavirus (HPV). They are common on hands and feet and can spread by contact.
symptoms: Pain when walking for plantar warts
precautions: Avoid picking or shaving over warts
Keep feet dry and wear sandals in shared showers
warts.when_to_see_doctor: See a doctor for warts on the face or genitals, if they bleed, change, or if you have diabetes or low immunity.

medicines.name: Salicylic acid 17% solution/plaster
medicines.usage_note: Applied daily after soaking and gently filing.
medicines.caution: Avoid healthy skin; not for face.

medicines.name: Cryotherapy (clinic procedure)
medicines.caution: May blister; several sessions may be needed.

urticaria.overview: Urticaria causes raised, itchy welts that appear and fade, often within hours. Triggers include foods, medicines, infections, heat or pressure.
symptoms: Welts that change shape or move
urticaria.when_to_see_doctor: Seek urgent care for swelling of the tongue or throat, difficulty breathing, or dizziness.

medicines.name: Cetirizine or loratadine (non-sedating antihistamine)
medicines.caution: Check dose for children and in pregnancy.

medicines.name: Calamine lotion
medicines.caution: For symptom relief only.

seborrheic_dermatitis.overview: Seborrheic dermatitis causes flaky, greasy scales and redness on oily areas such as the scalp (dandruff), eyebrows, sides of the nose and chest.
precautions: Avoid heavy oils on affected areas
seborrheic_dermatitis.when_to_see_doctor: See a doctor if it spreads, is very red or painful, or does not respond to shampoos.

medicines.name: Ketoconazole 2% shampoo
medicines.usage_note: Lathered and left for a few minutes, two to three times weekly.
medicines.caution: Avoid contact with eyes.

medicines.name: Zinc pyrithione or selenium sulfide shampoo
medicines.caution: May dry hair.

scabies.overview: Scabies is a contagious infestation by tiny mites that burrow into the skin, causing intense itching that is often worse at night.
precautions: Treat all household contacts at the same time
Wash bedding and clothes in hot water
scabies.when_to_see_doctor: See a doctor to confirm diagnosis and get treatment for the whole household.

medicines.name: Permethrin 5% cream
medicines.usage_note: Applied neck-down and washed off after 8–14 hours; often repeated after 1 week.
medicines.caution: All contacts must be treated simultaneously.

medicines.name: Oral ivermectin
medicines.caution: Not for young children or pregnancy without advice.

impetigo.overview: Impetigo is a contagious bacterial skin infection, common in children, producing red sores that burst and form honey-coloured crusts.
symptoms: Red sores around nose and mouth
precautions: Do not share towels; wash hands often
impetigo.when_to_see_doctor: See a doctor promptly; antibiotics are usually needed, especially if widespread or with fever.

medicines.name: Fusidic acid 2% or mupirocin 2% cream
medicines.caution: Complete the full course.

medicines.name: Oral antibiotics
medicines.caution: Only as prescribed.

pigmentation_disorder.overview: Pigmentation disorders change skin colour, causing lighter patches (such as vitiligo) or darker patches (such as melasma or post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation). Sun exposure, hormones, inflammation and genetics can all play a role.
symptoms: Lighter or darker patches of skin
Patches that change with sun exposure
precautions: Avoid bleaching creams of unknown content
Do not pick or irritate the area
Note any changes in size or colour
pigmentation_disorder.when_to_see_doctor: See a dermatologist to identify the exact type, especially if patches spread quickly or a mole-like spot changes shape or colour.

medicines.name: Broad-spectrum sunscreen SPF 50
medicines.usage_note: Daily protection prevents darkening and sunburn of light patches.
medicines.caution: Reapply every 2–3 hours outdoors.

medicines.name: Azelaic acid 15–20%
medicines.caution: May sting at first.

medicines.name: Topical corticosteroid or tacrolimus
medicines.caution: Only under dermatologist supervision.

contact_dermatitis.overview: Contact dermatitis is a red, itchy rash caused by something that touches the skin — an irritant (soaps, detergents, chemicals) or an allergen (nickel, fragrances, hair dye, plants).
symptoms: Red, itchy rash where the skin touched the trigger
Blisters or oozing in stronger reactions
precautions: Wash the area with mild soap and water
contact_dermatitis.when_to_see_doctor: See a doctor if the rash is widespread, on the face or genitals, shows signs of infection, or doesn't improve within 2 weeks.

medicines.name: Hydrocortisone 1% cream
medicines.caution: Avoid prolonged use on the face.

medicines.name: Calamine lotion or cool compresses
medicines.caution: Symptom relief only.

medicines.name: Oral antihistamine (e.g. cetirizine)
medicines.caution: Can cause drowsiness.
